#6379. Hubble spots a ghostly trail that may lead back to two shattered worlds

Hubble’s first visible-light view of the Cat’s Tail near Beta Pictoris offers clues to a possible collision between two large icy worlds.

Near the young star Beta Pictoris, a long streak of dust reflects so little starlight that it had escaped detection in visible light, the kind our eyes can see.

Now the Hubble Space Telescope has caught it for the first time. Its faintness fits dark, carbon-rich dust left over from a crash between two worlds at least about the size of Pluto’s moon Charon.

Beta Pictoris is about 65 light-years from Earth and roughly 18.5 million years old.

It’s still surrounded by rubble left over from building its planets, and astronomers nicknamed the streak the Cat’s Tail when they first spotted it in 2024.

The James Webb Space Telescope first revealed the tail in infrared light emitted by its warm dust.

Arin Avsar, a doctoral student at the Lunar and Planetary Laboratory of the University of Arizona, led the new study.

“The Cat’s Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies – think something like Pluto,” Avsar said.

“Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while.”

Avsar’s team stacked Hubble images taken in six rounds between 2012 and 2025. The result is the deepest Hubble picture of the system so far, but the signal is still weak.

Near its tip, the tail is barely brighter than the surrounding dust.

In visible light, the Cat’s Tail is roughly 200 to 1,000 times fainter than it looks to Webb in infrared.

“We think the Cat’s Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it’s made of,” Avsar said.

“It consists almost entirely of what we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they’re quite black.”

The team tested that idea with computer models of dust grains made from different mixtures. Rocky grains are made of the same kinds of minerals found in Earth’s crust.

A tail made mostly of them would have been about 100 to 10,000 times brighter in visible light than what Hubble recorded.

Dust that was 85% to 99% carbon-rich material by weight, with a little rock mixed in, matched best. Webb’s earlier infrared measurements had found the same thing.

Avsar’s team also checked that no single round of observations had created the tail by mistake. They left out one round at a time and rebuilt the image.

The tail showed up every time, though it got noisier near the tip.

The dust isn’t only dark. The models also showed that each grain is extremely porous, with somewhere between 55% and 93% of its volume taken up by empty space.

Dark, fluffy dust grains this tiny are an odd combination.

“How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that’s part of why we study this feature,” Avsar said.

What turned a young planetary body into fluffy dust is still a matter of speculation, Avsar added.

Kevin Wagner, a co-author and a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at the university’s Steward Observatory, offered one possibility.

“It’s possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that’s how they became so porous,” Wagner said.

The Webb team that found the tail in 2024 estimated that the crash behind it happened roughly 100 to 200 years ago. That team also calculated how much carbon-rich dust the tail holds.

Avsar’s team then asked how big the colliding bodies had to be to supply that much carbon.

Using measurements of a comet, the dwarf planet Haumea, and the dust that drifts between stars, they settled on a range of 14% to 38% carbon-rich material by weight.

Depending on the assumed carbon content, the team calculated a minimum diameter of roughly 750 to 1,000 miles (1,200 to 1,600 kilometers) for each body.

That’s about the size of Charon or Makemake, two icy worlds in the Kuiper Belt, the region beyond Neptune where Pluto orbits.

These are minimum sizes, rather than estimates of the bodies’ most likely sizes.

The team assumed the debris was equally dense at every size, but the tail’s fluffy grains are much less dense than solid chunks, so the real bodies were likely bigger.

The carbon most likely came from deep inside them.

Pluto’s reddish surface is coated with similar material, but that coating holds far too little of it to build a tail like this one.

Webb’s pictures are flat, like any photo, so they can’t show how far the tail stretches toward or away from us.

Astronomers measure distances like this in astronomical units, the average distance between Earth and the sun, about 93 million miles (150 million kilometers).

Visible light helps here. Dust scatters visible light differently depending on the angle between the star, the dust, and the telescope.

The heat it gives off looks the same from every angle. Comparing the two telescopes’ views let Avsar’s team estimate that angle.

“We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat’s Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it,” Avsar said.

“It’s essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it.”

The team’s models can’t settle it completely. They lean slightly toward a tail that extends somewhat behind the star. But they can’t rule out a tail in the same plane as the star, as seen from Earth.

A faint cloud of fine dust, called a halo, surrounds the disk above and below its flat middle.

With the new images, Hubble traced the disk out to about 500 astronomical units from the star, roughly 46 billion miles (75 billion kilometers), for the first time.

Telescopes on the ground had mapped that halo in 1995, but Hubble’s view is about 20 times sharper.

The sharper images show the halo is lopsided and warped. On one side it bulges outward above the disk, and on the other side it bulges below.

The disk’s main layer has a similar warp, and earlier studies traced it to Beta Pictoris b, a giant planet whose orbit is tilted compared with the disk.

Avsar’s team suggested that the same planet, or possibly the recently found planet Beta Pictoris d, may shape the halo too.

“This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force,” Avsar said.

“It’s a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units.”

Confirming that will take computer models that include all three planets and the push of starlight on small grains, the authors wrote.

By one estimate, icy moons and dwarf planets in our solar system are about 45% to 70% rock by weight. Much of their carbon-rich material is mixed into their rocky cores.

A crash that smashed two of them apart should have released plenty of rock along with the carbon, yet the Cat’s Tail has almost none.

Starlight may have separated the debris. It pushes carbon-rich grains harder than rocky ones, so the two kinds could have ended up in different places.

The rock might be in other dusty clumps that Webb has already seen in the disk.

Hubble also picked up a faint smudge near a second, tilted disk around the star, too weak to tell whether it’s real dust or a flaw in the image.

Deeper Hubble observations planned for the system should settle that.

With more detailed models of how these grains scatter light, astronomers could also tell where the tail really points.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

New research shows that a powerful 2021 marsquake emanating from Valles Marineris — the largest canyon in the solar system — was triggered by unexpected movement in a fault line deep below the gigantic structure, revealing that tectonic activity can still occur on geologically "dead" worlds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mars' supersize Valles Marineris — the largest known canyon in the solar system — is still tectonically active even though the Red Planet is geologically "dead," new research on a previously record-breaking marsquake reveals.

On Aug. 25, 2021, NASA's InSight lander, which touched down on the Red Planet in 2018, detected a powerful marsquake, designated S0976a. The Martian equivalent of an earthquake reached magnitude 4.2, which, at the time, was the most powerful quake that InSight or any other Mars lander had ever seen. (Since then, a 4.7 magnitude marsquake in May 2022 knocked it off the top spot, but S0976a remains second on this list.)

Unlike most marsquakes, which have been minor tremors triggered by meteorite impacts near InSight, S0976a was a deep rumble that originated from the opposite side of Mars as the robotic seismologist, in the western half of Valles Marineris.

In the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Communications, researchers reanalyzed the seismic wave data of S0976a and found that the quake originated from within a fault line running below the enormous canyon. The most likely explanation, they argue, is that there was tectonic movement in this hidden crustal crack.

"Valles Marineris is one of the most spectacular geological structures anywhere in the solar system, but until now we didn't know for certain that its faults are still active," study first author Jung-Hun Song, a researcher in the Department of Earth Science and Engineering at Imperial College London, said in a statement. "What we see is that this is not just a 'dead' fossil landscape, as faults deep beneath the canyon can still slip and generate marsquakes, long after the geological processes that originally formed them have ceased."

S0976a is the second-largest marsquake ever detected by NASA's InSight lander, shown here in a NASA clean room on April 30, 2015.

Valles Marineris is an enormous set of interconnected gullies and ravines stretching up to 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) in length, or roughly 10 times longer than the Grand Canyon. It is also up to 20 times wider and five times deeper, meaning that if you found yourself stranded at the bottom, it could take you a couple of months to climb out again.

The enormous chasm — named after the Mariner 9 spacecraft, which helped discover it in 1971 — is clearly visible from space, like a giant scar carved into the Red Planet's face. From orbit, you would also see the nearby Tharsis region, which is home to Mars' giant volcanoes, including Olympus Mons, which is at least three times taller than Mount Everest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

These imposing structures are proof that Mars was once geologically active, perhaps even more so than Earth. However, scientists think the Red Planet's surface has remained relatively unchanged for nearly 3 billion years, according to the European Space Agency.

Valles Marineris is almost as long as the continental U.S. is wide. (In this photo, captured by NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter, an optical illusion known as relief inversion may make the canyon appear as if it is raised above the surface, which it is not.)

The reason for this is twofold. First, Mars is smaller than Earth, so its core and mantle have cooled much faster than our planet's and are, therefore, less dynamic. Second, Mars has no tectonic plates. Instead of giant patches of crust butting against each other, the Red Planet's outermost layer is almost completely intact and acts like a giant lid over its cooling molten innards. (Research published earlier this week throws the "dead" theory into question, hinting that magma may still lurk below dormant Martian volcanoes).

Despite this, Mars still has fault lines. But rather than being a boundary between tectonic plates, these lines are more like giant cracks in its crust, some of which are visible at the surface.

In the new study, researchers discovered proof of what they call a slip-strike marsquake, where "blocks of crust move horizontally past one another along a steep, deeply rooted fault," the team said. They believe this occurred somewhere between 12 and 25 miles (20 to 40 km) below Valles Marineris.

The researchers also simulated several other potential causes of the marsquake, including a major asteroid strike or a landslide within the canyon, but nothing else could explain the patterns they saw.

Using seismic wave data captured by InSight, researchers were able to pinpoint the epicenter of the S0976a masquake (represented as a yellow star near the top of this map).

"What makes the result compelling is that several completely different types of evidence point in the same direction," Song said.

The finding also raises hopes that similar tectonic activity could one day be detected on other worlds across the solar system.

"Our study opens up exciting possibilities for discovering ongoing seismic activity on other planetary bodies that we might otherwise consider geologically inactive," Song said.

The discovery highlights the importance of detecting and studying marsquakes, which were only officially discovered in 2019, thanks to InSight. (Scientists have since uncovered older marsquakes, using data collected by the Viking landers in the late 1970s.)

InSight sent back a final selfie to Earth on Dec. 19, 2022, showing a heavy coating of Martian dust on its solar panels. Its mission was officially ended two days later.

"S0976a has turned out to be an extraordinary event," study co-author Doyeon Kim, head of Imperial College London's Terrestrial and Planetary Seismology Lab, said in the statement. "Its waves traveled through the core and helped us investigate the deepest part of Mars, and now they are telling us what happened at the source itself. From a single marsquake, we can learn both about the center of the planet and about an active fault beneath one of its most remarkable landscapes."

Scientists have similarly used marsquake vibrations from InSight to map out Mars' interior, leading to several intriguing subsurface discoveries, including dozens of blobs left over from ancient protoplanets, the hidden cause of the planet's uneven hemispheres, a potentially active "mantle plume" and a gigantic underground water reservoir containing enough liquid to cover Mars with a mile-deep (1.6 km) ocean.

Unfortunately, in December 2022, InSight quite literally bit the dust: A thick covering of Martian powder blocked its solar panels, preventing the lander from returning signals to Earth and thus ending its mission.

This means we currently have no way of detecting new marsquakes. However, the new study proves that the lander's archived data can still lead to exciting discoveries.

Song, J., Kim, D., Kolawole, F., Davis, J. M., Parry, R., & Maguire, R. (2026). Active crustal straining and fault reactivation at Valles Marineris. Nature Communications, 17(1). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78193-6

#6377. Scientists make the case for a specific year when human activity began transforming Earth, calling it the ‘Anthropocene epoch’

Scientists argue the Anthropocene began in 1952, separating a sharp global transformation from thousands of years of human influence.

Evidence of lead pollution and soil changes caused by early humans can be found buried in the earth dating back thousands of years ago. But when did human activity begin transforming Earth on a truly global scale?

A group of 37 researchers argues that early human impacts and the planet’s recent transformation are different stories.

Using one name for both, they write, obscures how sharply conditions changed in the mid-20th century.

They propose reserving “Anthropocene” for a geological epoch beginning in 1952, while giving the longer history of human influence a separate name.

The argument appears as a perspective piece, built on published evidence rather than a new dataset. Its lead author is Jan Zalasiewicz of the University of Leicester, who co-chairs the Anthropocene Working Group.

Co-authors include Buhm Soon Park of KAIST in South Korea, Julia Adeney Thomas of the University of Notre Dame, and Jürgen Renn of Germany’s Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology.

“The Anthropocene is a common language for understanding how rapidly and extensively humans are changing the Earth,” Park said.

“By clarifying its meaning and criteria, we can compare changes in the global environment more accurately and discuss together how we should respond.”

The relatively stable climate of the Holocene, which began about 11,700 years ago, helped people develop farming and build cities.

The authors’ case is that this stability ended in the middle of the 20th century.

That period saw the postwar surge of industry, population, and consumption known as the Great Acceleration.

The surge left marks in mud and ice. Across sites around the world, the chemical and physical traces of human activity pile up in layers centered on 1952.

That is also the year fallout from the first hydrogen bomb test settled across the globe. Those layers are the evidence the proposal rests on.

Humanity has used more energy since the 1950s than in the whole of the Holocene before it, most of it from fossil fuels.

A formal proposal to add the Anthropocene to the geological time scale, starting in 1952, went to the International Commission on Stratigraphy in October 2023.

The commission rejected it in March 2024, amid disagreement over whether an epoch only seven decades old was too brief to count.

The rejection did not retire the word, and the authors sort its uses into two families.

The meaning they defend is a geological epoch beginning when the Earth system stopped behaving as it had during the Holocene.

The other, which they call the extended Anthropocene, gathers up every substantial human impact over tens of thousands of years, from the earliest reshaping of ecosystems to the steam engine.

Proposed starting points have ranged widely. Some put it at 1784, when James Watt improved the steam engine.

Others point to European colonization of the Americas in the 1600s, or to farmed soils thousands of years earlier.

The authors call the extended version a valid idea but a different one. It can’t be pinned to a layer of rock, so the “-cene” ending, which marks a geological epoch, doesn’t fit it.

They suggest a separate label, such as “anthroposphere,” to keep the two apart.

The authors’ table of changes since the 1950s reads like an inventory of a different planet. Global freshwater use rose more than 300%, and the water held behind dams rose 1,500%.

Those dams are one reason rivers now deliver half as much sediment to the sea as they did.

The changes also reshaped marine and terrestrial life.

Predatory marine fish have declined about 90% since 1950 as the global catch quadrupled, and coral reefs, kelp forests, and mangroves have each lost about half their extent.

Humans and their livestock now make up about 98% of the mass of mammals on land, a shift other researchers have described as pushing life toward a mass extinction.

The authors lean on the planetary boundaries framework, which sets safe limits for nine Earth processes against pre-1950s Holocene baselines.

Seven of the nine have been crossed. That framework already treats the 1950s as the dividing line, they wrote, and a formal epoch would make that comparison standard.

Whether the commission will vote again is open, and the authors call formal recognition an ongoing aim.

The evidence keeps growing as new sites are analyzed, they wrote, from ocean chemistry to the plastics and persistent pollutants piling up in modern sediments.

They also acknowledged that a formal name on the time scale would not, by itself, make other fields adopt it.

In the scenario the authors describe, atmospheric carbon dioxide would still approach 500 parts per million even if the world reaches net zero carbon dioxide emissions by 2050.

Most polar sea ice and coral reefs would be lost, and sea level rise would keep accelerating.

Their research priorities are tracking heat, acidity, and plastics through the oceans, and pinning down the planetary boundaries and the tipping points behind them.

For now, 1952 remains a proposed boundary, and the Anthropocene remains a term with more than one meaning.

The perspective was published in the journal Nature Reviews Earth & Environment.

#6375. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6374. Early galaxies in the newborn universe spread elements like carbon and oxygen way faster than anyone expected

Webb found carbon, oxygen and silicon in moving gas around young galaxies, so heavy elements had already spread just 500 million years after the Big Bang.

In its first moments, the Universe held almost nothing but hydrogen and helium. Carbon, oxygen and other heavy elements came later, made inside stars.

Yet those elements had already spread into the gas around a galaxy seen just 500 million years after the Big Bang, and around two others seen a little later.

So the recycling that carries material from one generation of stars to the next was already working in at least some galaxies. The Universe was less than 4 percent of its present age.

Yongda Zhu, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Arizona and its Steward Observatory, led the work with colleagues there and at UC Riverside and the University of Michigan. Their sample is three bright galaxies, so the team can’t yet say how typical those galaxies were.

Light carries a record of whatever it passes through. Each element absorbs its own set of colors, and those colors show up as thin dark gaps when the light is spread out into a spectrum.

Zhu’s team used the starlight from each galaxy as its own light source. On its way to Earth, that light crossed the gas around the galaxy, and the gas left its gaps behind.

Catching gaps this faint took NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope. The light had been traveling for more than 13 billion years, and Webb collected it for about 29 hours with the setting that captured those colors.

All three came from a deep Webb survey of one patch of sky, and they were the only galaxies in it bright enough for this kind of measurement. The team chose them on brightness alone, before checking for any gaps, and all three turned out to have them.

The gaps matched oxygen, carbon and silicon. Some of the oxygen atoms were intact. Some of the silicon and carbon atoms had lost one electron, and others had lost three, which takes harsher, more energetic conditions.

All of those versions showed up at overlapping speeds. A single calm cloud of gas inside a galaxy would have a hard time producing that mix. It points instead to gas in several states, moving together and tied to each galaxy.

The pattern of gaps looked broadly like the one astronomers see in star-forming galaxies from more than a billion years later. Elements like these went on to build later stars and rocky planets.

In an interview with Earth.com, Zhu tied the moving gas to stellar feedback – the push that massive stars and their explosions give the gas around them.

“You can picture young galaxies as both factories and distributors,” he said. “Stars inside them produce elements such as carbon, oxygen, and silicon, and stellar feedback then pushes some of this enriched gas outward.”

The gaps didn’t land exactly where they would for gas at rest alongside each galaxy. They were shifted slightly toward bluer colors, which happens when gas is moving toward the telescope.

The gas lay between each galaxy and Earth, so moving toward Earth meant moving away from the galaxy. The shifts match speeds of roughly 31 to 155 miles per second (50 to 250 kilometers per second). Even the low end would cross the continental United States in about a minute and a half.

“In our JWST spectra, we see this gas moving relative to the galaxies themselves, showing that these elements were already being spread into their surroundings,” Zhu said.

The speeds can’t show how far out the gas reached. A wind blowing close to a galaxy and gas spread farther around it would produce the same shift, and churning motions inside the galaxy could add to it.

The most heavily stripped atoms may have been moving faster than the rest, but sharper spectra will be needed to confirm that.

Webb had already found heavy elements inside galaxies even older than these three, including oxygen in one of the most distant galaxies known.

Outside galaxies, most earlier measurements came from later times. They relied on light from extremely bright, distant galaxy cores shining through random stretches of gas, which were only loosely connected to any one galaxy.

“The speed of the process was the most striking part,” Zhu told Earth.com.

“Previous JWST observations had already shown that very early galaxies could produce heavy elements, but our results show that galaxies were also beginning to redistribute those elements into their environments remarkably early.”

The very first stars would have formed from pure hydrogen and helium. Astronomers have spent years looking for them, and they’ve proved hard to find.

Zhu said the result may help explain why. Once the first generations of stars began enriching their surroundings, he said, “chemically pristine environments may have disappeared rapidly.”

The heavy elements needn’t have come mostly from those first stars, though. Other researchers’ models show that a later generation of stars, with some reaching 200 to 300 times the mass of the Sun, could make carbon and oxygen this quickly.

Three bright galaxies can’t show how common this was. Some other gas clouds seen in the early universe hold almost no heavy elements, so the spreading was probably patchy, reaching some places well before others.

At this level of detail, Webb’s spectra also blur fine structure, and the team couldn’t map where the gas ends. An actively feeding black hole in one of the galaxies can’t be fully ruled out either, though the spectra show no clear sign of black hole activity.

“The next major question is how common this process was,” Zhu said. He wants deeper observations of more galaxies, to learn whether outward-moving enriched gas was common in the early universe. Sharper spectra could also separate the motions of the gas in its different states.

For now, the finding rests on three of the brightest galaxies of their time. Larger samples will show whether the rest of the young universe was spreading its elements just as early.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

#6373. Wanting a digital detox may reveal something unexpected about you

A new study explores why people want a digital detox and how their attitudes relate to self-control, mindfulness, and screen habits.

Eighty-one percent of people feel positive about the idea of putting down their phones and stepping away from screens for a while.

But here’s the twist: that desire to unplug has almost nothing to do with being addicted to technology.

People who score high on wanting a digital detox aren’t the ones doom-scrolling at 2 a.m. They’re the mindful, self-controlled types who’ve simply decided their attention is worth protecting.

A team from Goethe University Frankfurt and the University of Bath has developed and validated the first psychometric scale for measuring attitudes toward digital detox.

The Attitude toward Digital Detox (ADD) scale is a seven-item questionnaire. Participants rate their agreement with statements like “Reducing my digital activities improves my mental health.”

Rated on a 1-to-7 scale, the measure captures how favorably someone views the idea of temporarily dialing down their digital consumption.

Digital detox, as the researchers define it, is fundamentally different from technology avoidance.

Avoiding technology means permanently rejecting a specific device or platform because it’s too complex, too inflexible, or not worth the switching costs.

A digital detox attitude is something else entirely. It’s a conscious, temporary inclination toward balance.

The development process was exhaustive. The participants were a mix of US adults recruited online and Central European university students.

Across seven studies, the team started by asking 157 participants to generate statements describing both attitudes toward and behaviors around digital detox. That produced 628 candidate items.

Consumer behavior experts from universities including Tübingen, Bocconi, Cologne, Passau, and St. Gallen then rated each item for representativeness and comprehensibility.

The pool shrank to 72, then 27 after content validity screening.

Finally, it went down to seven items after exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses on 400 participants.

The resulting scale showed strong internal consistency and only weak correlation with social desirability.

People weren’t just saying what sounded virtuous.

Study 4 tested the scale against a web of related psychological constructs using 382 US adults. The correlations painted a clear picture  and some of it was genuinely unexpected.

Self-control correlated positively with ADD scores. So did mindfulness and holding a growth mindset about intelligence.

People who believe their cognitive abilities can develop were more favorable toward stepping away from screens.

All of that tracks with the idea that digital detox attitudes emerge from a proactive appraisal process. People consciously evaluate their digital consumption and decide they’d benefit from less of it.

What didn’t correlate was more revealing. Perceived stress showed no significant relationship with ADD.

Neither did pathological internet use or smartphone addiction. These findings suggest that the desire to unplug extends beyond people experiencing problematic technology use.

“Being able to reliably measure that attitude opens the door to understanding what makes people more receptive to stepping back from technology, how those attitudes develop and whether they ultimately translate into changes in digital behavior,” said study co-author Lisa Eckmann.

In a pre-registered study with 1,583 US adults, participants chose a video genre they enjoyed and then alternated between watching clips and doing word-search puzzles.

Afterward, they could freely choose to watch another video or do another puzzle. People scoring higher on the ADD scale spent significantly less time watching each video.

However, ADD scores didn’t predict whether participants chose another video or another puzzle.

More favorable attitudes were associated with shorter viewing times, suggesting a connection with how long people engaged rather than whether they started.

Two additional validation studies tested whether the scale could distinguish between groups with predictably different orientations toward screens.

Members of Reddit communities focused on reducing screen time or using paper journals, such as r/nosurf and r/bulletjournal, scored significantly higher on the ADD scale than members of technology-focused communities such as r/ebooks and r/SmartThings.

The gap was large: 5.33 versus 3.47 on the seven-point scale.

Among Central European university students surveyed during the pandemic, those who preferred face-to-face teaching scored markedly higher on the detox scale.

And their attitudes predicted real behavior. Higher ADD scores correlated with actually attending more lectures in person over the winter term.

The researchers grounded the scale in Lazarus and Folkman’s transactional model of stress and coping.

The framework proposes that when people repeatedly experience digital consumption as taxing, they begin to view disengagement as a way to cope.

Over time, those experiences may develop into a more stable attitude.

That’s what the ADD scale measures: the crystallized disposition, not the momentary frustration.

One practical implication is immediate. People who score high on digital device usage time score lower on the ADD scale.

That negative correlation was statistically significant. The attitude does seem to connect, however loosely, to how much time people actually spend online.

But the researchers are careful to note that the attitude-behavior gap in digital consumption is well documented. Screen-time tracking apps reliably raise awareness of heavy usage.

They rarely produce sustained behavior change.

The scale opens several doors. Marketers could use it to identify consumers receptive to intentional disengagement and design experiences accordingly.

Researchers can now investigate whether there’s a subjective tipping point where digital consumption tips from manageable into overload.

And in a landscape increasingly shaped by AI-driven personalization and algorithmically curated feeds designed to maximize engagement, the question of who wants to opt out – and why – is only going to get more pressing.

The study is published in the journal Psychology & Marketing.

#6371. A tiny protein ring reveals how cells keep DNA under control

Scientists filmed a tiny protein complex changing shape and gripping DNA, revealing how it captures and holds different DNA segments.

A textbook draws DNA as a tidy spiral staircase. Inside a living cell, though, it is forever being copied, strained, broken, and patched, and proteins do the handling.

A new study has filmed a protein complex called Smc5/6 at work.

The ring-shaped complex swings open and shut, closes around DNA, and sometimes holds two DNA segments at once.

Kenichi Umeda and Noriyuki Kodera of the Nano Life Science Institute at Kanazawa University in Japan led the work with Yasuto Murayama of the National Institute of Genetics.

They watched purified protein from baker’s yeast, outside any cell, so what they saw is the machine running on a bench rather than inside a living nucleus.

“By observing individual Smc5/6 structures as they interacted with DNA, we could see how changes in their shape are associated with different ways of capturing and holding DNA,” Umeda said.

“These observations bring us closer to understanding how this protein assembly carries out its roles in maintaining chromosomes.”

Smc5/6 belongs to a small family of ring-shaped complexes that organize chromosomes, the bundles that carry a cell’s DNA.

Its job is clearing away DNA structures that would jam cell division, such as stalled copying machinery and strands twisted around each other. Cells need it to divide correctly.

Earlier methods gave either a frozen snapshot of its shape or a record of its movement with no structural detail. The Kanazawa team used a microscope that works by touch.

It drags a needle tip far finer than a hair across the sample and records a new image every 0.5 to 1.5 seconds.

The complex has two long arms connected by a hinge at one end and a pair of motor domains at the other. These motor domains break down ATP, the cell’s energy currency.

Lying flat, the complex measured about 38 nanometers from hinge to motors. A human hair is more than a thousand times wider.

Without fuel, more than 80% of the complexes had their arms close together, about 5 nanometers apart at the middle. The team called this shape the I-form.

Add ATP and some of them swung open into a ring, the O-form, with the arms 19 nanometers apart.

About 60% of complexes with a mutation that allows ATP binding but prevents its breakdown were open.

So binding the fuel opens the ring, and using it up lets the arms fall back together.

The team saw single complexes flip between the two shapes as they watched.

One small subunit, Nse2, is attached partway along one arm like a splint.

Without it, a few complexes bent their arms sharply toward each other, a shape never seen when Nse2 was present.

Other complexes in the same protein family are known to fold at an elbow this way, so the splint may be what keeps Smc5/6 straight.

Loading the complex onto a loop of DNA about 1,900 letters long required both ATP and a pair of helper subunits. Once on, the ring slid freely along the strand.

The team observed two ways the complex gripped DNA.

About half of the normal complexes held the strand at the hinge end, swaying as they did so. The rest gripped it at the motor end and stayed rigid, tilted at about 73 degrees to the DNA.

The mutant that can’t burn ATP almost always gripped at the motor end. Breaking down the fuel therefore appears to help move DNA from one compartment of the ring to the other.

The two grips were also associated with different DNA bends.

DNA held at the hinge curved by a median of 110 degrees at the contact point, while DNA held at the motor end bent less than 50 degrees.

When Smc5/6 was bound to a relaxed circle of DNA, the circle shrank.

The team measured how spread out each DNA loop was.

Loops carrying the protein were about 6% more compact on average, and loops the protein had pulled into a twisted shape were about 30% more compact.

The twisted loops more often carried more than one complex.

In 33 of 38 twisted loops with multiple complexes, two sections of DNA stayed pinned together for about 100 consecutive frames.

A separate test on magnetic beads confirmed it. With ATP present, the protein tethered about 25% of free DNA circles to DNA fixed on the beads, compared with under 3% without ATP.

Cutting either DNA circle once released the other, suggesting that the protein ring encircled both.

The mutant that can’t break down ATP tethered DNA just as well, suggesting that holding two DNA segments requires ATP binding but not its breakdown.

That sets tethering apart from a better-known trick of this protein family, reeling DNA into loops, which runs on a steady supply of ATP.

The experiments used purified yeast protein and bare DNA, without the crowding, other proteins, or ongoing repair activity found inside a real nucleus.

The authors wrote that their case for DNA being enclosed within a closed protein ring rests on several converging lines of evidence rather than a direct chemical proof.

The sharply bent form appeared in only 3% of complexes lacking Nse2.

The team said the microscope’s surface may have held the molecules too flat to show how often it really occurs. Nor can the imaging rule out that some closed-looking complexes were open rings standing on edge.

The next question is whether Nse2 does more than keep the arms straight. Does it also help control how the complex pulls DNA into loops?

The team will need to film the complex while it builds a loop to find out.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

Using machine learning, astronomers developed a new way of looking at James Webb telescope data that allows far-off planets to emerge from their star's glare.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it comes to spotting planets orbiting distant stars, the biggest hurdle is often separating the signal from the noise — specifically, trying to distinguish a planet from the stellar glare around it. That's true even for the most sophisticated telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

Now, astronomers have developed a new way to spot planets that were formerly drowned out in a sea of light. Using a combination of modeling and machine learning techniques, they picked out a previously hidden giant exoplanet in data from JWST. The results were published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

"Planets are a million times fainter than their stars," study first author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, an astronomer at Northwestern University, said in a statement. "So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare."

Telescopes like JWST use instruments called coronagraphs to block out some of this excess light, similar to the way the moon and a pinhole camera operate during a total solar eclipse. But even the best coronagraphs have limitations — for example, they can't block all the glare, and the telescopes themselves move.

Even the most stable telescopes vibrate almost imperceptibly as they collect light, so the images a telescope produces contain ever-so-slight mismatches compared with what the instrument actually sees. These slight shifts can be enough to obscure even very large exoplanets.

To address this, Ferrer-Chavez and his team developed a "digital twin" of JWST that virtually recreates how light travels through the telescope's detectors, minus any movement-based imperfections. To fine-tune this digital replica, the researchers used computational models based in real-world physics alongside machine learning techniques similar to those used to train AI. But the authors stressed that this is not an AI model.

"Because we already know the physics, we don't need AI to understand what's happening," study co-author Jason Wang, also an astrophysicist at Northwestern, said in a statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP.

Using FLIP, the team analyzed data from three stars, including 51 Eridani, which is located around 97 light-years from Earth and was already suspected to have a giant exoplanet orbiting it. Although the planet, called 51 Eridani b, had been detected by ground-based telescopes, it was drowned out by light in previous JWST observations. With FLIP, however, 51 Eridani b popped out from the dataset.

The scientists hope this approach will help astronomers pick out even more hard-to-spot exoplanets, especially ones that look like the planets in our own backyard. In the nearly 35-year history of exoplanet hunting, the vast majority of planets we've found have been radically different from those in our own solar system, partially because larger and more reflective worlds are easier to spot with current telescopes.

"It's not that [solar-system-like planets] don't exist," Ferrer-Chavez said. "It's that we can't see them."

Ferrer-Chavez, R., Wang, J. J., Bouman, K. L., Freeman, W. T., Pueyo, L., Feng, B. Y., & Perrin, M. D. (2026). Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit. Nature, 659(8139), 58–62. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z

#6369. Tiny populations are challenging what we know about wildlife recovery

Species reduced to fewer than 50 wild individuals can still recover, a study finds, challenging assumptions about their chances of survival.

In 1974, the Mauritius kestrel was down to just four known birds in the wild.

Conservation textbooks practically wrote the obituary. Half a century later, the Mauritius kestrel numbers in the hundreds.

A team led by Donal Smith at Monash University, working with researchers from the Zoological Society of London, has now tracked every bird and mammal species that dropped below 50 individuals in the wild at any point since 1950.

The findings deliver an empirically grounded gut punch to one of conservation’s most persistent – and most dangerous – assumptions: that tiny populations are doomed.

The theory sounds airtight. When a population gets critically small, bad things compound.

Inbreeding depression. Loss of genetic diversity. Random demographic swings that can wipe out a handful of animals in one bad season.

Biologists call this the “extinction vortex” – a feedback loop that supposedly drags small populations toward zero with increasing speed. Influential thresholds emerged.

Traditional genetic guidelines suggested effective population sizes of 50 to limit short-term inbreeding and 500 to maintain long-term evolutionary potential.

These figures describe the population’s genetic contribution to future generations, rather than a simple count of animals.

The team set out to test that assumption across a comprehensive set of bird and mammal species.

Smith’s team identified 147 bird and mammal species – 98 birds and 49 mammals – known to have fallen below 50 wild individuals since 1950.

Of these, 141 had enough time elapsed to assess an outcome.

The researchers classified every conservation action each species received into three categories.

Limiting factor mitigation covers efforts to remove whatever is driving the decline – predator control, habitat restoration, supplementary feeding.

Population manipulation acts directly on the species itself through captive breeding, translocation, or egg fostering.

Indirect action includes the softer tools: legal protections, public awareness campaigns, designating national parks.

Then they ran Bayesian multi-level logistic regression models to see what actually predicted recovery.

Of those 141 species, 39 went extinct. That’s 28 percent – a grim reminder that the extinction crisis is real.

But 33 species recovered to populations of 100 or more. Recovery was strongly associated with direct conservation action.

Among the 51 species that received direct conservation action, 61 percent recovered to at least 100 individuals.

Among the 90 species that received no direct action, just 2 percent recovered. And 37 percent went extinct.

“Our work shows that population size alone shouldn’t determine whether we give up on a species,” Smith said.

The Bayesian models put hard numbers on it. Limiting factor mitigation carried an odds ratio of 8.71 for recovery to 100 or more individuals. Population manipulation had an odds ratio of 5.53.

The two together were even stronger: predicted probability of recovery hit 74 percent for birds and 71 percent for mammals when both action types were deployed.

Without either? Six percent for birds. Five percent for mammals.

The median time to recovery was 18 years. Eight species clawed back from populations below 20.

The Lord Howe woodhen might be the study’s most dramatic illustration.

Endemic to tiny Lord Howe Island in the Tasman Sea, the species was hammered by feral pigs, cats, and rodents after European arrival.

By the late 1970s, an estimated 23 birds remained. Conservationists launched a captive breeding program while eradicating pigs and cats.

Captive breeding and the removal of introduced predators helped the population recover to around 200 birds.

Following the 2019 rodent eradication campaign, numbers rose sharply, reaching an estimated minimum of 1,638 by late 2024.

Here’s what makes the findings politically charged. Conservation triage – the idea that some species are too far gone to justify spending on – has influenced real decisions.

The baiji, the Yangtze River dolphin, is the study’s starkest cautionary tale. Active conservation efforts were scaled back. The species went extinct.

But Smith’s team found surprisingly little evidence of deliberate triage actually driving extinctions. What they found instead was worse: indecision.

The Christmas Island pipistrelle was monitored for over a decade before anyone intervened. By then it was too late. Decision paralysis, not cold calculation, was the killer.

The urgency isn’t theoretical. While the study was being prepared, avian malaria was driving two Hawaiian honeycreepers – the ‘akikiki and the ‘akeke’e – toward the same cliff edge.

The ‘akikiki’s wild population had collapsed to an estimated four non-captive individuals by 2024. A captive breeding program established in 2015 is its lifeline.

The ‘akeke’e, whose population has dropped below 100, depends on whether malaria can be controlled. Recent genomics-informed modelling suggests it can survive – if the threat is addressed.

The paper is careful to note what recovery actually means. Many “recovered” species still require intensive management.

Island invasive species eradication demands permanent biosecurity. Large mammals may need anti-poaching protection indefinitely.

Captive breeding programs often maintain insurance populations for decades. Recovery, in other words, is not a finish line. It’s a commitment.

The findings challenge the idea that a critically small population is, by itself, a reason to abandon conservation efforts.

As the authors put it: predictions of extinction as an inevitable fate may be self-fulfilling.

We’re probably fortunate that so many determined conservationists refused to believe them.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

#6368. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

#6367. The 8 Best Air Purifiers for Your Home

Whether you’re dealing with smoke or pet dander, these are the most effective (and affordable) models we stand behind based on testing and research.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Clean indoor air has become more important than ever. While allergens like dust, dander, mold, and bacteria are all teaming up to infiltrate the air you breathe, the widespread wildfire smoke affecting much of the U.S. right now is also proving just how quickly outdoor pollution can make its way inside. According to the EPA, Americans spend about 90 percent of their time indoors, where pollutant concentrations can sometimes be even higher than they are outside. An air purifier protects your airways from airborne irritants while providing clean, fresh air indoors (which is why we think everyone should invest in an air purifier).

We got our hands on air purifiers from brands like Coway, Levoit, and GermGuardian and put them to the test. Filtration was our main concern, so we could determine the air purifiers’ efficiency. Then we moved along to other factors such as noise while running, how well they work in a given room, and convenience features. After our in-home testing, these are the air purifiers that came out on top.

We tried out several air purifiers with a range of filtration systems, noise levels, and features. We tested these models in multiple different apartments, placing them in various rooms of the home to measure their efficiency. We considered the different uses of an air purifier, like if you’re an allergy sufferer or have a home filled with furry friends, and tested special features like light-up displays and automatic shutoff to determine their ease of use and effectiveness. We considered the amount of time it took to set up the different purifiers and install their filter systems.

For units that we haven’t tested, we combed through dozens of potential products and their specifications, reviews, and user complaints to identify what we thought were the best air purifiers. We settled on the following list, which includes options that are budget-friendly, sleekly designed, and high-performing.

The Airmega Mighty2 is the latest version of our previous Best Overall pick, the Coway AP-1512HH. The newest model combines power, quality filters, and robust controls to help you breathe easier.

The Mighty2 uses a three-stage filtration system to capture 99.7 percent of airborne particles, and cleans spaces up to 1,800 square feet in 60 minutes. It has three standard fan speeds, but there’s a turbo mode that will kick on if there’s a big uptick of matter in the air.

The original version just used an indicator light system that let you know basic air quality levels, but this updated model has a built-in air quality index sensor that measures and displays particulate matter counts in real time.

Our tester tried the air purifier in his New York apartment, putting it up against pet odors, litterbox dust, and other household allergens. “Results after about a day were already noticeable. The air in the room seemed clearer and there was less dust on the ground in the area immediately around the litterbox. Not enough that I’m going to have to sweep up any less, mind you, but there was a material difference that I wasn’t getting from using a smaller purifier.”

Full Coway Airmega Mighty2 Air Purifier Review

This air purifier from Clorox uses a three-stage filtration system to trap allergens, pollutants, and VOCs, and it successfully cleared strong scents and odors from the apartment we tested in.

It was quiet enough that you hardly hear it activate, especially if it kicks on automatically while you’re cooking to clear the kitchen of smoke. But on higher settings, you do tend to notice its noise a bit more. The 360-degree, cylindrical shape of the filter offers purification from all directions, and the unit covers 1,000 square feet so you don't have to be as strategic about placement.

We also liked that it has a color-coded indicator light on the front that tells you how hazardous the air is in the room where it's located (though it will add insult to injury when it turns purple while you’re trying your best to sear a steak.)

If you’re a pet owner, specifically with cats, then you know that the litter box smell lingers long after your little fur ball has left the lavatory. The Vital 200S-P from Levoit is a great way to combat the odors that candles and air fresheners just can’t cover up. I set the air purifier up in my living room and noticed a clear improvement in scent after running for the day.

This unit has a traditional air inlet, along with a unique U-shaped inlet that is ideal for trapping pet hair without clogging up the filters. If you pair your air purifier with the app and select Pet Mode, it automatically alternates between fan speeds, too. The pre-filter is easy to remove and wash, so you don't have to purchase replacements as often.

Since we tested the Vital 200S-P in a smaller apartment, it was a bit obtrusive. But the air purifier covers up to 1,875 square feet, so if you live in a townhouse or single-family home, this unit will accommodate.

Full Levoit Vital 200S-P Air Purifier Review

The Airmega 100 is the first cylindrical unit in the Coway line, which is a nice switch-up from the rectangular model that we tested in the past. It tucked nicely into the corner of the living room, and you can change the light between blue, orange, and off, which is ideal if you’re using the purifier in a bedroom.

I tried the fan on various settings, and the lowest mode could barely be heard over the TV playing at an average volume, which aligns with its claimed 20-decibel noise level. You can manually adjust everything on the control panel, or let the purifier do its thing and adapt accordingly as it monitors the air quality of the room.

Setup of the unit was simple; you essentially just need to click the filter into place. This model uses a 3-in-1 filtration system, with a HEPA filter sandwiched between a vacuumable pre-filter and deodorizing filter. The deodorizer layer is especially useful if you have pets, love to cook, or live in an apartment or complex with odors.

Full Coway Airmega 100 Air Purifier Review

For smaller rooms or office spaces, the smart Blueair 511i Max offers much of the same performance and features as larger, more capable models. It only purifies areas of up to 465 square feet, but does so within just 30 minutes on the highest setting. The three-layer filtration system captures up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles, too.

We appreciate that the air quality level is clearly displayed on the front in a five-color scale, and that the display has auto-brightness controls if you're running it overnight while you're sleeping. Advanced features are available through the app, including scheduling and air quality reports.

This unit has a four-stage filtration system, along with Blueair's proprietary HEPASilent filter that uses a combination of electrostatic charge and mechanical filtration to capture 99.97 percent of airborne pollutants and contaminants. This type of filtration technology is less dense than other filter options, so it's designed to run quieter and use less energy.

The value offered by such a small air purifier is unmatched, considering it targets both allergens and odors—all with relatively quiet operation.

If you have a large space or even an entire apartment that needs air purification, the Coway Airmega 400 is the smart model you need. It's designed to cover up to 1,560 square feet in 30 minutes, and has a variety of smart features and sleep settings, all packed into a compact yet capable unit. While this is the most expensive option we recommend, it's relatively affordable considering its capacity, and you shouldn’t have to supplement with an additional air purifier.

It’s surprisingly quiet given its size, reaching only 22 decibels on its lowest setting. We like that it uses multi-stage purification methods, combining a pre-filter, an activated carbon filter, and a True HEPA filter to capture the tiniest of particles. The pre-filter is washable, but the air filter indicator light will let you know when it actually needs to be replaced.

The Airmega 400 has a three-setting smart mode that adapts to its environment, with a fan speed that automatically adjusts based on air quality or lighting conditions. We also appreciate the option to use eco mode, which turns the fan on and off when the room has remained purified for 30 minutes, and there’s also a timer and pollution sensor.

The GermGuardian isn’t a flashy design with robust features, but it aids in keeping the air in my apartment free of pet odors, dust, and smoke.

I have a self-cleaning litter box, which significantly cuts down on smells and dust associated with cat waste, but it doesn’t solve every problem. I let the purifier run during one of the Litter Robot’s cleaning cycles, and thanks to the GermGuardian’s built-in air quality index (AQI) sensor and display screen, I was able to see the particulate matter count in the air reach triple digits in seconds. The automatic fan speed varied as needed, and it wasn’t long before air quality was back to a healthy level.

I put the GermGuardian up against incense smoke, too, and it went to work quickly. The fan had to run at high speed for longer, but by the end, my living room was clear of any lingering haze and odor.

In addition to a HEPA filter and activated carbon, this model also has a UVC light, which is claimed to disinfect bacteria, viruses, and mold. While I did give this feature a try, I didn’t keep it on for long because it’s hard to prove whether these lights are actually useful in an air purifier.

Read Full GermGuardian AC4880B Air Purifier Review

The Sans HEPA 13 air purifier offers quiet operation, whole-home purification, and smart features. This unit runs at only 25 decibels on the lowest fan setting, and I could hardly tell that it was on, even when standing next to the unit.

The air purifier is best used for whole-home use, as it purifies spaces up to 1,854 square feet. The internal sensors monitor and show you the air quality index in real time, and the reading is visible on the touch display. I’m able to view PM2.5, which is particles that are 2.5 microns or smaller, such as dust, smoke, pollen, and pet dander, as well as PM10, which are slightly larger particles up to 10 microns, like coarser dust and mold spores.

This unit pairs a medical-grade HEPA 13 filter with a pre-filter, activated carbon filter, and UV-C light to capture 99.9 percent of particles. This might be overkill for general household use, but I’ve appreciated the multi-stage approach. The only downside I’ve come across is that overall cost will likely be higher, considering the Sans recommends replacing the filter every three months.

There is no shortage of air purifiers on the market, and many of them use a lot of the same tech to achieve better air quality. We’re often testing many different models to find the top recommendations. Ahead are some that haven’t made it to this roundup, but are still worth considering.

Rabbit Air A3 Air Purifier: This air purifier uses a six-stage filtration system to rid your home of smoke, dander, odors, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and germs. The lowest fan setting clocks in around 20 decibels, which is extremely quiet, so you can run this model daily without being disturbed. The build is relatively bulky so it’s not the easiest to tuck into a corner and out of the way, and the $760 price tag is pretty steep.

GermGuardian AirSafe+ XL: This model is shaped like our best portable pick above, and comes with a lot of the same features as the other GermGuardian we recommend, and it has a companion app for tracking air quality metrics. That said, the app doesn’t specify what type or size particulate matter the sensor is measuring, so it’s hard to tell what common allergens are actually floating around your home.

Air purifiers vary in filtration range, so it's important to first consider your room size before buying. To find a model that accommodates your space, the EPA recommends that you first multiply the length and width of the area where you intend to operate the air purifier to calculate the square footage.

Most air purifiers have a maximum coverage area listed, so just compare to your calculations to find an air purifier that is the best fit for your home.

If you have an open floor plan or high ceilings, opt for an air purifier with more coverage. You should also place the air purifier in the room you use most regularly, and make sure it’s in an area where the airflow isn’t obstructed.

The filter system of your air purifier might differ depending on the model and issue you're trying to target such as allergy relief, odor elimination, or germ protection. You’ll often see three-stage filtration (or four-, five-, or six-stage), which includes all three of the filter types detailed below.

Pre-filters are typically the first line of defense in an air purifier and trap larger particles like dust, hair, and fur, which helps extend the lifespan of the main filter and improves the overall efficiency of the unit.

All of our selections on this list involve a multi-step filtration system to target a majority of common pollutants and allergens in your household.

Purvi Parikh, MD, an allergist and immunologist with NYU Langone Health, recommends selecting an air purifier that comes with a HEPA filter. “Make sure it's a HEPA air purifier since these filter down to 0.3 microns and have a robust amount of studies done showing their efficacy.” HEPA filters remove at least 99.97 percent of airborne particles like dust, bacteria, and pollen, and are the gold standard for air purification.

Activated carbon filters are more porous and help get rid of gases and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are commonly found in household items like surface cleaners and candles. These filters absorb molecules onto carbon and are best used in environments with strong odors or smoke.

With laundry machines, dishwashers, and fans all emitting their own noise, adding another loud appliance into the mix could be overkill, especially since air purifiers are meant to run the entire day.

Look for models that range from 10 to 30 decibels. A whisper is around 30 decibels, so expect air purifiers in this noise range to be almost virtually silent.

“Air purifiers need to be kept clean, and filters should be changed every six months,” Parikh says. Since air purifier filters are designed to collect and trap different-sized particles, contaminants, and hair, they get gunky pretty easily. This buildup could even reduce the efficiency and the air quality of the purifier if not cleaned often enough. Most air purifiers come with reusable filters, so just rinse them off in between replacements.

App compatibility, savvy control panels, remotes, check filter indicators, and variable settings are beneficial features that make it easier to use your air purifier. If you want to monitor the air quality levels in your home or keep tabs on filter life, look for an air purifier that pairs with an app. If you’re easily overstimulated by loud noises, consider an air purifier that has different modes for adjusting the speed of the internal fan.

Air purifiers use a fan to draw air into the unit, then pass it through a series of filters to remove particles and contaminants. Said filters vary in effectiveness and normally target a specific concern like odors, smoke, and viruses. Once the air has passed through the fan and all of the appropriate filters, it is recirculated back into the room for a cleaner and healthier environment.

“Air purifiers filter out pollutants, improve air quality, remove infectious agents and pollen,” says Parikh. “They limit your level of exposure and reduce lung damage and flare-ups of underlying chronic conditions such as asthma attacks, COPD exacerbations, and heart issues.”

“It can affect everyone’s health by causing inflammation and lung damage over time that may be either reversible or irreversible,” Parikh says. “It is especially dangerous for those with underlying heart disease, lung disease, pregnant women, children, and immunocompromised individuals.”

#6366. Monterrey’s mountain folds tell a story millions of years in the making

An astronaut photograph reveals Monterrey’s sweeping mountain ridges, where ancient rock folds shape the landscape around a growing Mexican city.

Monterrey has spread across the plains of northeastern Mexico, but its mountains leave little room for straight lines.

Long ridges bend beside the city, tracing folds in the rock that formed tens of millions of years before streets and factories occupied the landscape.

Today’s Image of the Day captures this meeting of urban growth and ancient geology.

Photographed from the International Space Station on August 26, 2026, the scene shows Monterrey alongside the sweeping ridges of the Sierra Madre Oriental.

From the ground, these mountains form a familiar skyline.

From orbit, their repeating curves reveal a much larger pattern: a landscape compressed, lifted, and gradually carved into the terrain that surrounds the city today.

The ridges along Monterrey’s southern edge began as layers of sediment that became limestone during the late Mesozoic era.

Their present shape developed much later, as forces within Earth’s crust squeezed and folded the rock.

Mountain building in the region occurred roughly 80 million to 50 million years ago.

Rather than remaining flat, the layers buckled into a series of folds, creating the foundation of the parallel ridges visible today.

Erosion then changed the relief. Over millions of years, weaker layers wore away more readily than resistant rock, helping turn the folded formations into distinct ridges and valleys.

That sequence explains why the mountains appear to follow one another across the landscape. Their curves reflect related layers shaped by the same broad episode of deformation.

The photograph offers a view of both processes at once. Folding established the pattern in the rock; erosion made that pattern more apparent at the surface.

Monterrey is the capital of Nuevo León and a major center of Mexican industry.

Steelmaking and ironworks form part of an economy that also produces glass, plastics, textiles, and processed foods.

Its metropolitan area had about 5.3 million residents in the 2020 census. That figure describes the wider urban region, rather than just the municipality of Monterrey.

The city occupies a semiarid floodplain beside the mountains. As development spreads, the contrast between the built environment and the surrounding terrain becomes especially striking.

A city map can show roads and municipal boundaries. This view from space adds another set of boundaries: steep slopes, narrow valleys, and rocky ridges that influence where development can extend.

The mountains are more than a backdrop to Monterrey. Their position helps define the shape of the urban area, bringing ancient geological structures directly into the geography of everyday life.

The Río Santa Catarina connects the mountain landscape with the city below. After cutting through the Sierra Madre Oriental, it crosses the urban area and carries runoff from its watershed.

For much of the time, the river holds little water or appears dry. In this semiarid setting, however, a quiet channel still has an essential function.

Summer rainfall can send substantial volumes of water through it. The channel provides a route for that runoff to move across the metropolitan area.

It also supports living communities within the city. Vegetation along the river provides habitat for plants and animals and creates connections through an otherwise heavily developed landscape.

Part of the river channel in the metropolitan area received state protection as an urban park in 2008. Its value extends across seasons, serving wildlife even when little flowing water is visible.

Separate mountain masses also rise beside Monterrey’s urban neighborhoods. Among them is Sierra Las Mitras, a protected ridge that reaches approximately 4,900 feet above the city.

Its slopes hold a changing sequence of habitats. Cacti and thorny shrubs occupy lower, rocky ground, while cooler, wetter conditions support oak and pine forests higher up.

That change shows how elevation can create different environments within a relatively small area. The journey uphill passes through habitats that contrast sharply with the dry terrain below.

Cerro de la Silla, known for its saddle-shaped profile, adds another distinctive landmark to Monterrey’s mountain setting.

As Monterrey expands, its ancient ridges continue to shape the city’s boundaries and guide its growth.
